Evaluating Self-Generated Documents for Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Large Language Models

Jiatao Li, Xinyu Hu, Xunjian Yin, Xiaojun Wan

Peking University

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗

Documents generated by a model can help retrieval-augmented answers, but their usefulness depends on document style, model capacity, and how they are combined with retrieved evidence.

Result
CCU documents plus style-transformed Wikipedia average 53.6 (EM/F1, Qwen2.5-32B), vs 52.1 for GenRead Direct Mix and 45.6 for Wikipedia alone.
New vs prior
GenRead (Yu et al., 2023) generates background documents instead of retrieving them; this work asks which document types and mixing strategies help.
Limitation
Human evaluation checks only style adherence; the authors note that the factual accuracy of self-generated documents cannot be guaranteed.
01 / The research question

Generated context is a representation choice

Self-generated documents (Self-Docs) are passages a model writes from its own parametric memory before answering. They draw on no external source; they externalize what the generator can already produce, which may make useful facts easier to use. If the source is generated rather than retrieved, which properties of that text decide whether it helps?

The paper treats the document type as an experimental variable. A detailed formal report and a conversational overview can share facts yet suit different tasks: fact verification needs specific evidence, while a long-form explanation needs coverage and organization.

Closest prior work

Generation-augmented methods such as GenRead (Yu et al., 2023) and recitation-augmented models (Sun et al., 2023) have a model write background passages before answering, and hybrid approaches (Zhang et al., 2023; Abdallah and Jatowt, 2024) merge generated with retrieved documents. The paper notes that this work has mostly focused on how to use such documents, for example how to handle conflicting knowledge, while overlooking how different types of generated documents affect performance. It therefore classifies Self-Docs with a Systemic Functional Linguistics taxonomy and reuses GenRead's pipeline as its generator.

02 / Inside the method

Generator size, document type, and mixing are tested separately

The experiments first separate three factors that are otherwise confounded: the size of the base model, which both writes and answers; the number of documents; and the size of the generator alone, with the answerer fixed at Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. Documents come from GenRead's few-shot pipeline, whose examples are drawn from k-means clusters of query–document pairs.

The taxonomy, grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics, crosses three binary choices: tone (Authoritative or Conversational), granularity (Fine- or Coarse-grained), and structure (Structured or Unstructured). Types are named by these initials: AFU is authoritative, fine-grained, and unstructured (the paper's example is a case study), CFU a personal essay, and CCU a social media post.

Finally, Direct Mix concatenates retrieved Wikipedia passages with Self-Docs, while Style-Transformation Mix first has an LLM rewrite the passages in the Self-Docs' style. Because the rewrite is itself a model step, a gain belongs to the whole pipeline, not to the retrieved content alone.

  1. 01

    Vary capacity and quantity

    Compare document generators and answering models at different sizes, then vary how many generated documents enter the context.

  2. 02

    Separate document properties

    Use a linguistics-based taxonomy of tone, detail, and structure to form eight document types for controlled comparisons.

  3. 03

    Combine information sources

    Compare direct mixing with Wikipedia passages against transforming their style before combining them with generated documents.

Types and examples: Section 5.1 and Table 4; document openings from Figure 1 and Appendix G.2, shortened. Comparisons are computed here from the per-type rows.

Gains are task-specific. Relative to the same documents alone, Style-Transformation Mix gains most on multi-hop HotpotQA and fact-verification FEVER and leaves long-form ELI5 essentially unchanged. Among generated types, unstructured documents beat structured ones on average, authoritative fine-grained ones suit FEVER, and conversational ones suit ELI5.

Scale effects are also uneven. A larger generator helps only above a size threshold; smaller generators struggle to beat either answering without documents or Wikipedia retrieval. More documents help FEVER, while ELI5 may plateau or dip.

Scope. Main experiments use Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and 500 examples per task across four datasets. Generated documents can contain factual errors, and effective styles vary with task and model. Read the study ↗

Read the abstract

The integration of documents generated by LLMs themselves (Self-Docs) alongside retrieved documents has emerged as a promising strategy for retrieval-augmented generation systems. However, previous research primarily focuses on optimizing the use of Self-Docs, with their inherent properties remaining underexplored. To bridge this gap, we first investigate the overall effectiveness of Self-Docs, identifying key factors that shape their contribution to RAG performance (RQ1). Building on these insights, we develop a taxonomy grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics to compare the influence of various Self-Docs categories (RQ2) and explore strategies for combining them with external sources (RQ3). Our findings reveal which types of Self-Docs are most beneficial and offer practical guidelines for leveraging them to achieve significant improvements in knowledge-intensive question answering tasks.
